newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir car bomb mars India-Pakistan talks.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir car bomb mars India-Pakistan talks.

text.p: A car bomb explosion in India's Jammu and Kashmir state on Saturday underscored the tensions in the volatile Himalayan region that could prove to be a stumbling block in landmark talks between India and Pakistan.
At least 14 people were killed and more than 50 injured when the bomb went off in a crowded bus station in Jammu, the winter capital of Jammu and Kashmir.
Senior Indian and Pakistani diplomats who ended a second day of talks declined to comment on whether they had narrowed differences over Kashmir.

Asked if authorities had any clues on who planted the bomb, Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Farooq Abdullah told Reuters by telephone: "There are a number of people who do not want the talks to succeed. We strongly condemn this attack. Innocent people have died. Terrorism must stop."
In Srinagar, the state's summer capital, police said they fired warning shots in the air to disperse a small group of Kashmiri separatists protesting at the India-Pakistan talks.

"The biggest thing is that the talks have started," Abdullah said. "I don't expect miraculous success in one go. At least there's a thaw, the ice has started to melt. It is a 50-year-old problem, it won't settle down in one meeting."
Pakistan's foreign secretary Shamshad Ahmad and his Indian opposite number Salman Haidar made only brief comments after their three rounds of talks.

"I shall rapidly withdraw from the realm of forecasting," Haidar said when asked if he expected a breakthrough. Ahmad, asked if he was optimistic about the outcome, said: "We diplomats are always hopeful."

Pakistan's foreign ministry spokesman, Khalid Saleem, said the delegations would meet again on Sunday. "All substantive issues came in for further discussion," he said. "Kashmir is an integral part of the discussions."
The two sides have pledged to make no public comment until their discussions, due to end on Monday, are over.

But the Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency said Ahmad told Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda that Pakistan would not put the thorny Kashmir dispute on hold while the two countries tackled other problems.
"There has to be some meaningful progress on the core issue of Kashmir before we address other matters," PTI quoted him as saying. His reported remarks could not be confirmed.

The talks are the first since January, 1994, when a dialogue foundered on Kashmir. Tensions over the sparked two of the three wars between the two countries, now threshold nuclear powers, since independence in 1947.

India accuses Pakistan of arming Moslem rebels fighting in the two thirds of Kashmir under Indian control. Pakistan, which holds the rest of Kashmir, denies the charge but says it supports the Kashmiris politicallly.
Mirwaiz Omar Farooq, leader of Kashmir's All Parties Hurriyat (freedom) Conference, criticised India and Pakistan for excluding Kashmiris from any discussions on their future.
"We don't see this as a bilateral issue," he told Reuters by telephone. "It's not a territorial or regional dispute they can discuss by themselves...The Kashmiris must be involved."
The governor of Jammu and Kashmir, K.V. Krishna Rao, said Pakistan should show its sincerity by reining in the guerrillas.

"Pakistan should stop infiltrating militants into Kashmir and hand over the Kashmiri youths undergoing training in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir to India to give peace a chance to flourish," PTI quoted him as telling 200 former militants who have joined the paramilitary border security force.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in Kashmir since the start of an armed revolt there in January 1990.
